transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-04-10 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~58m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Redwood), Priya Reddy (Neptune ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Neptune Infra), Maya Chen (Neptune Research), Tom Becker (Neptune CTO)
Shared: https://redwood.com/benchmarks/neptune-quant-run-20260410.xlsx, https://docs.redwood.ai/security/soc2.pdf

Summary (auto): Quick run through of quantization options. Customer cares about preserving 99th-percentile latency under 120ms and <2% accuracy regression on classification/eval set.

00:00 Speaker 1: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we can kick off
00:12 Sofia (Redwood AE): Hi all, im Sofia from Redwood, i'll be the AE, joined by Daniel our SE. today we want to walk through the quantization tradeoffs — int8, fp8, g p t q and a w q — and how those interact with kv cache and batching for your usecase
00:28 Daniel (Redwood SE): quick intro, i'm Daniel, i've been looking at Neptune's perf summary you sent over, and ran an initial awq pass on a 13B style model — i will caveat the transcription, some of the numbers are still preliminary
00:45 Priya (Neptune): thanks, our main asks: tight tail latency (p99 < 120ms) for chat inference, maintain less than ~2% hit on our intent classification accuracy after quantization, and we have to run inside our VPC on prem hardware
01:10 Liam (Neptune): infra side, we have 4xA40-equivalent nodes with 80GB host memory, and we want to avoid excessive KV cache spill to host. network is 25Gbps between nodes. we'll need guidance on sizing
01:30 Daniel (Redwood SE): good, that helps. some top-level notes: INT8 often gives best throughput but higher accuracy regressions unless you use per-layer or groupwise scaling; GPTQ tends to preserve accuracy but can be slow during compile; AWQ is a newer method with better out-of-the-box fp-like accuracy for some LLMs but results vary
02:05 Maya (Neptune): can you unpack the difference between g p t q and a-w-q? we saw both in the literature but not sure about production implications
02:15 Daniel: sure — g p t q (g p t q) is typically a post-training quantization algorithm that does per-layer or per-channel weight quant with a reconstruction step using a small calibration set; it often reduces accuracy loss at the cost of a heavier offline compile. AWQ (a w q) tries to optimize quantization-aware weight reconstruction per-block and can produce better FP-like results for certain attention-heavy layers. caveat: naming gets messy in transcription, so the acronyms might be transcribed oddly
03:00 Tom (Neptune CTO): what's the runtime differnce, like compile time vs inference time? we prefer shorter rollout time
03:10 Daniel: compile is the offline step — g p t q compiles can take minutes to hours depending on model size and calibration samples. runtime inference cost is mostly the same across quant methods once the kernels are generated, but AWQ-optimized kernels might require special codepaths which our runtime can select. INT8 optimized kernels are the fastest in pure throughput in our tests
03:45 Priya: any notes about fp8? i've read FP8 can preserve activations better but hardware support is limited
03:55 Daniel: correct — FP8 gives better dynamic range for activations and can reduce quantization noise, but it needs hardware/driver support (nvidia upcoming drivers, some proprietary silicon supports FP8). if hardware supports it, FP8 can be a great middle ground for accuracy vs perf
04:20 Liam: how does the KV cache behave under quantization? will quantizing weights break cache format or increase memory for KV?
04:30 Daniel: KV cache stores activations, so weight quantization doesn't directly change stored KV size, but there are interactions: some runtimes compress KV or store in fused formats; if you quantize activations (activation quant), you'd alter KV size/precision. also, int8 quant kernels may keep KV in fp16 internally for stability which still consumes similar memory
05:05 Priya: we saw a ~3.5% drop on our customer prompts with int8 earlier using naive scaling, can that be reduced?
05:15 Daniel: yes, naive static per-tensor scaling often causes regressions. recommended: per-channel or per-block scales, calibration with representative prompts (1k samples is good), and targeted higher-precision for sensitive layers (first/last n layers or attention/query/key/value projection layers). that's what g p t q and awq try to address
05:50 Maya: what's the perf delta p99 vs avg latency when you batch? we can't blow up tail latency
06:00 Daniel: batching increases throughput but can hurt p99. continuous batching (our runtime) groups similar lengths and has timeouts to bound p99; also prefix caching helps. for chat workloads, small batch sizes (2-8) and dynamic batching with deadline heuristics tend to preserve p99 while still improving throughput
06:35 Liam: any tips on preventing KV cache spilling to host?
06:40 Daniel: size ROI: ensure per-request sequence length budgeting, reserve GPU memory for KV based on worst-case seq length, and use compact KV formats. Redwood's runtime can pre-allocate KV arenas per worker to avoid fragmentation. if host spills happen, p99 jumps dramatically
07:05 Priya: when you say "per-layer higher precision" is that like hybrid quant where some layers stay in fp16? how do you pick them?
07:15 Daniel: exactly — hybrid or mixed-precision. pick layers via sensitivity analysis: run layerwise ablations on a small eval set, score impact. attention output, first few embeddings, and final norm/projection layers often are sensitive. our tooling automates this scanning and suggests a profile to keep error under target
08:00 Speaker 2: there's a mention in the doc about activation clipping, can you say more
08:05 Daniel: activation clipping or dynamic range calibration constrains activation outliers which would otherwise blow scales. you pick clipping thresholds via percentile stats (e.g., 99.9th) from calibration runs; it's a tradeoff between quant noise and saturations. some AWQ variants do adaptive clipping per-block
08:40 Priya: are there known cases where AWQ introduced regressions though? we want to avoid surprises in safety prompts
08:48 Daniel: yes, AWQ can be brittle on models with unusual weight distributions or small-dataset calibration. best practice: validate on safety/prompt set and keep a fallback model (e.g., fp16 or g p t q profile) in rollout. Redwood supports rollout policies to route fractional traffic to fallback if metrics degrade
09:20 Tom: about on-prem/VPC: what's the control plane behavior? we need audit logs and KMS integration for keys
09:30 Sofia (Redwood AE): for Private deployments we offer a customer-controlled control plane with KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. we'll share SOC2 and architecture docs. Neptune will maintain their VPC peering and we'll provide peering checklist
09:50 Liam: what about kernel/driver versions for FP8? do we need special drivers on our on-prem?
09:58 Daniel: yes, some FP8 kernels need recent NVIDIA drivers and specific cuBLAS/cutlass versions. we'll provide a compatibility matrix. for INT8/GPTQ/AWQ, our runtime supports fallback kernels that run on slightly older drivers but with modest perf hit
10:25 Priya: ok for benchmarks, what should we send as calibration set?
10:30 Daniel: 1k representative prompts (diverse lengths), include safety/regression prompts and a devtest of 200 samples for quick perf/accuracy checks. include real-world chat logs (anonymized) if possible
10:55 Maya: any recommendations on monitoring after rollout for quant regressions?
11:00 Daniel: yes — establish automated evals on a holdout prompt set, track key metrics (accuracy delta, perplexity, safety troves). Redwood Optimize can run continuous evals and send alerts on regression > threshold (e.g., >1.5% drop)
11:30 Liam: what about batching knobs: do we tune timeout or max batch size?
11:35 Daniel: both. timeout set to balance latency vs throughput; max batch size tied to GPU memory and model size. we'll help tune with a small grid search during pilot
12:00 Priya: can you share a sample rollout plan for a canary?
12:05 Sofia: typical plan: 1) offline quant & validation, 2) deploy canary (1-5% traffic) on Dedicated, 3) monitor 48-72h for p99/accuracy/regressions, 4) progressively ramp to 25%/50%/100% with automated rollback on metric triggers. we'll include the exact metrics and thresholds in the doc we send
12:40 Tom: on cost side, what's rough % cost win for int8 vs fp16?
12:45 Daniel: roughly 2x throughput improvement or 40-60% cost reduction depending on parallelism and batching. FP8 sits in between. exact numbers depend on sequence length distribution and KV cache memory pressure
13:10 Priya: any gotchas with RAG or retrieval-augmented workflows?
13:18 Daniel: RAG increases context windows so KV memory grows; quantization helps with model memory but retrieval embeddings and doc store are separate. also watch for hallucination changes — quant regressions can slightly alter answer phrasing, so include RAG prompts in evals
13:50 Maya: ok let's talk pilot timeline — we can run pilot on Dedicated starting 2026-04-20 if you can provide the pilot config
13:58 Sofia: yes we'll prepare a pilot pack: required infra params, sample JOBs, telemetry queries. expecting ~1 week of tuning run and then a 2-week canary
14:20 Daniel: i'll run an initial microbenchmark with the prompts you send and share a CSV with latency/throughput and top-k accuracy numbers. link will be dropped into CRM and slack
14:45 Priya: any public docs or previous case studies we can read?
14:50 Sofia: we shared a benchmark spreadsheet and our SOC2 link — we'll also drop a case study on a similar 13B model that used hybrid g p t q + per-layer FP16 to hit <1% regression
15:05 Tom: final Q — if we see a regression post-rollout, what's the rollback cadence? immediate?
15:12 Sofia: we recommend immediate rollback for safety regressions; for small accuracy diffs we do staged rollback while investigating. Redwood's rollout engine supports instant traffic switchback to a previous model version
15:30 Recap (Sofia): action items: we'll share benchmarks and driver matrix; Daniel runs microbenchmarks; Priya/Liam to share calibration data and infra details; schedule pilot week starting 2026-04-20.
15:45 End of call

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-typing of acronyms (g p t q / a w q), speaker labels flattening to Speaker 1/2 in parts, and some numbers approximated in real time.
